Project documentsAnalysis plan Code

Scope and reporting framework
This document is the authoritative specification of the study’s scientific objectives, population, definitions, estimands and statistical methods. ARCHITECTURE.md documents the implementation, AGENTS.md the working conventions, and GitHub Issues the open decisions and implementation status. Neither file supersedes this plan.
Reporting will follow STROBE and RECORD1,2. The comparative analyses are specified as emulations of target trials3 and will also follow TARGET4. The reporting map links each checklist item to a section of this plan.

1. Objective
Single-center studies report fewer UTIs after methenamine initiation in kidney transplant recipients5–7. These were pre/post or uncontrolled comparisons. Prophylaxis is started when UTI frequency peaks, so a subsequent decline is expected from regression to the mean alone. In non-transplant women with recurrent UTI, a randomized trial found methenamine noninferior to daily antibiotic prophylaxis8,9. No randomized evidence exists in kidney transplant recipients.
Aim 1 (descriptive pharmacoepidemiology). Among kidney transplant recipients with Medicare Parts A, B and D, describe annual use of methenamine, prophylactic-dose antibiotics and vaginal estrogen from 2006 through the last complete claims year, overall and by transplant center, and before vs. after publication of the ALTAR trial (March 2022).
Aim 2 (primary comparative effectiveness). Among recipients who meet a claims-based recurrent-UTI definition, estimate the effect of initiating (a) methenamine, (b) prophylactic-dose antibiotics, or (c) neither within 30 days, on the 12-month number of treated UTI episodes and on UTI hospitalization.
Aim 3 (secondary). Estimate the effect of initiating vaginal estrogen vs. not among women with recurrent UTI (§8.3).
Aim 4 (descriptive). Reproduce the 2019 pre/post analysis with an explicit regression-to-the-mean reference (§8.4).
These are observational estimates subject to residual confounding by indication; §9 lists the safeguards and §3.2 the data limitations.
Out of scope. Phenotyping (autoencoders), individualized treatment rules (Q-learning, targeted learning) and cost-effectiveness from the Aim 2 text are deferred to a follow-on study. They depend on a validated version of the cohort, exposure and outcome definitions here and on adequate numbers within subgroups.

2. Design
Aims 2 and 3 are emulations of target trials of initiation strategies among recipients who meet a recurrent-UTI definition, analyzed by clone–censor–weight3,10. The target-trial protocol and how the emulation achieves each component are in Appendix A. Aims 1 and 4 are descriptive.

2.1 Relation to the 2019 protocol



2019 protocol / Aim 2 element
This plan




Pre/post Poisson regression with clustering as primary
Retained as a descriptive secondary analysis with a matched non-initiator reference that quantifies regression to the mean (§8.4)


Comparative analyses “if sufficiently powered”
Primary: target trial emulation of initiation strategies among recipients meeting a recurrent-UTI definition (§4–§8, Appendix A)


Methenamine and topical estrogen analyzed together
Methenamine vs. antibiotic prophylaxis vs. neither is the primary question; vaginal estrogen is a separate trial in women (§8.3)


Suppressive antibiotics as a group
Prophylactic-dose antibiotics defined by dose and supply, with TMP-SMX given for Pneumocystis prophylaxis handled explicitly (§5.3)


Autoencoder phenotypes, Q-learning, cost-effectiveness
Deferred to a later study that builds on this cohort (§1)


Claims 2006–2014/2017
All Part D years available in the analyzed release (Part D begins 2006)

3. Data source

3.1 Files and observation
Files: Core (patients, payer history, death, residence, facility), transplant files, institutional (inpatient and outpatient) and physician/supplier claims, Part D drug events (PDE) and Part D enrollment (PDENROL) for each available year from 2006. Skilled nursing, home health and hospice claims are not used for outcome ascertainment.
Eligible observation time for a person is the set of days on which all of the following hold: on or after a kidney transplant; Medicare FFS primary Parts A and B (MPAB); enrolled in a stand-alone Part D plan per L3; before the administrative end date (L13); and alive.
Lookback: 365 days of continuous eligible observation before time zero, used for eligibility, recurrent-UTI ascertainment, new-user status and covariates.


3.2 USRDS data limitations and how this plan handles them
This section is binding: definitions elsewhere in the plan are written to respect it. Confirm every item against the Researcher’s Guide and appendices for the specific release analyzed11.



#
Limitation
Consequence
Handling in this plan




L1
Claims exist only for Medicare fee-for-service periods. Medicare Advantage, Medicare-secondary-payer periods (including the employer coordination period), other insurance and uninsured periods produce no or incomplete claims. ESRD beneficiaries could newly enroll in Medicare Advantage from 2021, so the FFS share shrinks in recent years.
Missing UTIs, antibiotics and covariates outside FFS primary periods; selection toward FFS beneficiaries in recent years.
Require Medicare FFS primary Parts A and B (MPAB) for the entire lookback and censor at loss of MPAB (§3.1). Report the FFS share by calendar year. Broader MPAB+MPO as a sensitivity analysis.


L2
ESRD-based Medicare entitlement ends 36 months after a functioning transplant for beneficiaries who are not ≥65 or disabled.
Recurrent UTI often arises years after transplant; later-onset recurrent UTI is observable only among recipients who keep Medicare (older, disabled, graft failure). Follow-up is truncated for others.
Describe the cohort by basis of Medicare entitlement and time since transplant. Treat coverage loss as censoring and model it with inverse-probability-of-censoring weights (§8.2). State the restricted generalizability explicitly; do not present results as representing all recipients.


L3
Part D enrollment is separate from A/B and recorded monthly (PDENROL contract IDs). Months with MA-PD contracts have drug events but no FFS medical claims. Beneficiaries with retiree drug subsidy or other drug coverage have no PDE records.
Drug exposure is unobservable outside stand-alone Part D months; MA-PD months would yield drugs without outcomes.
Require continuous Part D enrollment, defined from monthly contract IDs, and MPAB on the same days. Allow at most one missing month inside a span (as in the Santos pipeline12); verify the contract-type codes for each release.


L4
PDE records dispensings paid through Part D. Cash purchases, discount-generic programs, samples, VA and other-payer fills do not appear. Inexpensive generics (nitrofurantoin, TMP-SMX, cephalexin, methenamine) are the most likely to be bought outside the plan.
Exposure misclassification, possibly differential by drug; under-ascertainment of treated outpatient UTIs.
Report fills per covered person-year by drug and year as a plausibility check. Sensitivity analysis restricting to low-income-subsidy enrollees (cost sharing near zero, so out-of-plan purchase is less likely). Interpret absolute UTI rates cautiously; prioritize the hospitalization outcome, which does not depend on PDE.


L5
PDE shows dispensing, not ingestion or indication. Unfilled prescriptions are invisible. Prophylaxis vs. treatment must be inferred from drug, dose and supply.
Misclassification of prophylactic vs. treatment courses.
Dose and supply rules for prophylaxis (§5.3); continuous-use episodes with prespecified grace periods (§5.4); sensitivity analyses varying the rules.


L6
Drugs given during inpatient stays are bundled into Part A and absent from PDE; some outpatient parenteral antibiotics appear only as HCPCS J-codes on Part B claims.
Treatment for hospitalized UTIs is not seen in PDE; a supply appears to “run out” during a stay.
Inpatient UTI episodes are identified from institutional claims, not drug data. Extend outpatient supply by the length of overlapping inpatient stays. Include Part B antibiotic HCPCS codes for outpatient treatment.


L7
Immunosuppressants for recipients whose transplant Medicare covered are billed largely under Part B (HCPCS J75xx), not Part D; the Part B immunosuppressive drug benefit began in 2023.
Immunosuppression is incompletely seen in PDE alone.
Ascertain maintenance immunosuppression from Part B HCPCS and PDE together, and from transplant-file induction and discharge regimens. Verify which claim files carry Part B drug claims in the release.


L8
The prescriber is an encrypted ID (PRSCRBRUSRD_ID); prescriber specialty is not available in PDE.
Cannot attribute initiation to urology, nephrology or infectious diseases.
Use urology and infectious-disease visits from physician/supplier specialty codes as covariates. Prescriber ID may support clustering and a prescriber-preference instrument (§9).


L9
No laboratory or microbiology data: no urine cultures, organisms, susceptibility or creatinine. Asymptomatic bacteriuria cannot be distinguished from symptomatic infection. Resistance codes (e.g., ICD-10-CM Z16) exist only after October 2015 and are under-coded.
UTI case definitions are imperfect; surveillance intensity varies by center.
Outpatient UTI requires a diagnosis plus antibiotic treatment (§7.1). Adjust for patient-level and center-level urine-culture billing (§5.5). Resistance outcomes are exploratory, ICD-10 era only.


L10
UTI diagnosis codes are nonspecific and can reflect rule-out encounters.
Outcome misclassification.
Require treatment for outpatient episodes; collapse codes within 14 days into one episode; report the inpatient principal-diagnosis outcome separately.


L11
Urologic risk factors (neurogenic bladder, reflux, stents, self-catheterization, prostatic disease) are inconsistently coded.
Residual confounding by indication.
Use them as covariates where coded; add a negative-control outcome (§9).


L12
Clinical transplant detail comes from transplant registration and follow-up forms (OPTN/UNOS-derived); post-transplant rejection treatment, immunosuppression changes and estimated GFR are incomplete.
Imperfect adjustment for net immunosuppression and graft function.
Use graft failure and retransplant dates from USRDS; rejection treatment from claims (e.g., thymoglobulin HCPCS) as a time-varying covariate where feasible.


L13
Data currency differs by file: claims, Part D and death dates have different end dates in each release.
Apparent loss to follow-up near the end of data.
Define an administrative end of follow-up as the earliest complete date across the claims, PDE and enrollment files used; mortality ascertainment is not equated with claims availability.


L14
ICD-9-CM to ICD-10-CM transition on 1 October 2015.
Discontinuities in coded conditions.
Era-specific code lists; outpatient/professional claims follow service date and inpatient claims follow discharge date13. Calendar period is a covariate; era-specific sensitivity estimates.


L15
Unapproved methenamine combination products (with methylene blue, phenyl salicylate and others; marketed for urinary symptom relief) may appear under methenamine generic names.
Misclassification of symptomatic analgesic use as prophylaxis.
Classify by NDC and generic name into single-agent methenamine hippurate, methenamine mandelate, and combination products; only single-agent products define exposure.


L16
Small cells. DUA disclosure rules.
Suppression of counts 1–10 and complementary cells.
Applied to all tables, figures and text; may limit center- and subgroup-level reporting (§10).





3.3 Prior use of these data
Preliminary work in an earlier release, with Part D claims for 2006–2014, found enough transplant recipients with Part D who filled methenamine or vaginal estrogen to proceed.

4. Study population
Adult (≥18 at transplant) kidney recipients with a functioning graft and eligible observation time (§3.1) who meet the criteria below.

Time since transplant. Time zero is ≥180 days after the most recent kidney transplant. Open: #1 180 days vs. 90 days.

Recurrent UTI. ≥2 treated UTI episodes (§7.1) within 180 days, or ≥3 within 365 days, with the qualifying episode on or after day 180 post-transplant. Episodes before the most recent transplant do not count.

New user. No fill of methenamine or prophylactic-dose antibiotic in the 365-day lookback. Recipients receiving TMP-SMX at Pneumocystis prophylaxis dosing at time zero are eligible; that exposure is a baseline covariate. Open: #2 alternatively exclude, or restrict to recipients ≥12 months post-transplant when PJP prophylaxis has usually stopped.

Exclusions at time zero. Dialysis or graft failure, pregnancy codes in the prior 280 days, chronic indwelling catheter or nephrostomy codes (sensitivity: include).
Repeated eligibility. The primary analysis uses each recipient’s first qualifying time zero. A sequential-trials sensitivity analysis uses every eligible qualifying episode, with robust variance by person.

5. Exposure and time zero

5.1 Methenamine
Single-agent methenamine hippurate or methenamine mandelate, identified by NDC and generic name (L15). Combination urinary analgesic products do not count.


5.2 Vaginal estrogen
Estradiol vaginal cream, tablets/inserts and low-dose ring, and conjugated estrogens vaginal cream. Systemic-dose vaginal rings (estradiol acetate) and oral/transdermal estrogens are excluded from exposure and recorded as covariates.


5.3 Prophylactic-dose antibiotics
An initiating fill with days supply ≥28 and a daily dose in the prophylactic range, for example nitrofurantoin ≤100 mg/day, cephalexin ≤500 mg/day, trimethoprim 100 mg/day, fosfomycin every 7–10 days, or TMP-SMX given as prophylaxis outside the PJP context. Daily dose = strength × quantity ÷ days supply, after collapsing same-day fills (§5.6). Initiation is classified from the first fill alone; later duration is not used to assign arms, because that would use future information.

Open: #3 final drug list and dose thresholds; whether TMP-SMX can ever count as UTI prophylaxis given identical PJP dosing.



5.4 Continuous-use episodes (per-protocol analyses)
Consecutive fills of the same agent form an episode when the gap after accounting for carried-over supply is ≤30 days. Supply is extended by overlapping inpatient days (L6). Discontinuation = episode end + grace period. Switching between strategies is a protocol deviation.

Open: #4 grace period of 15 days as in Santos et al.12, or 30 days.



5.5 Surveillance intensity
Patient level: number of urine culture claims (e.g., CPT 87086, 87088) in the lookback. Center level: mean annual urine cultures per recipient among Part D-covered recipients without a UTI diagnosis, by transplant center and year, as proposed in the Aim 2 text.


5.6 Dispensing records
Exclude non-oral dosage forms where relevant; require positive quantity and days supply; collapse same-day fills of the same drug by summing quantity and days supply. Strength is parsed from the drug record, with drug-specific prophylactic vs. treatment thresholds (§5.3).

Open: #5 whether to also require positive patient pay, as the Santos pipeline did12; that filter excludes $0 low-income-subsidy fills and is proposed to be dropped.



5.7 Time zero
The end date of the qualifying (second or third) treated UTI episode, on which the recurrent-UTI criterion (§4) is met.


5.8 Covariates
Measured at or before time zero unless noted: age, sex, race and ethnicity, calendar period, time since transplant, donor type, retransplant, diabetes, primary cause of kidney failure (including urologic), coded urologic abnormalities, prior UTI episode count and hospitalizations, prior resistant-organism code (ICD-10 era), prior C. difficile, immunosuppression class (L7), recent rejection treatment, TMP-SMX at PJP dosing, recent urology and infectious-disease visits, patient and center urine-culture intensity, low-income subsidy and dual eligibility, transplant center region. Time-varying covariates for weights: interim UTI episodes and hospitalization.

6. Comparators
Strategies, each started within 30 days of time zero: (A) start methenamine; (B) start prophylactic-dose antibiotics; (C) start neither. The A vs. B contrast is an active comparison of two prophylaxis decisions made at the same clinical juncture, reducing confounding by indication relative to A vs. C. Assignment is emulated by cloning each eligible person into all three strategies at time zero (§8.2); there is no matching.

7. Outcomes

7.1 Treated UTI episode (primary building block)
Inpatient. An inpatient stay with a UTI or pyelonephritis code in the principal position (sensitivity: any position).

Outpatient. An outpatient institutional or physician/supplier encounter with a UTI code (cystitis, pyelonephritis, UTI site unspecified, catheter-associated UTI) and a treatment-dose antibiotic fill or Part B antibiotic administration from day −3 to +5. Prophylaxis-dose fills do not count. Open: #6 the treatment window.

Episodes. Codes and treatment within 14 days are one episode; the episode date is its first code.


7.2 Primary outcome
Number of treated UTI episodes within 12 months after the 30-day grace period ends, summarized as the mean cumulative count with death as a competing event14.

Open: #7 whether the count starts at time zero or after the grace period; starting at time zero is preferred for the intention-to-initiate contrast.



7.3 Secondary outcomes
UTI hospitalization (principal diagnosis); urosepsis or bacteremia with a urinary source; days of treatment-dose antibiotic supply; Clostridioides difficile infection; all-cause hospitalization; graft failure; death; Medicare payments (via usRds cost functions, inflation-adjusted). Exploratory: fluconazole-treated candidiasis; resistant-organism codes (ICD-10 era only).


7.4 Follow-up and censoring
Follow-up runs 12 months from time zero, until the outcome count horizon, death, graft failure, retransplant, loss of eligible observation (§3.1), or the administrative end date (L13), with the censoring reason recorded.

8. Statistical analysis

8.1 Descriptive analysis (Aim 1)
Annual period prevalence of each exposure per 1,000 Part D-covered recipient-years, by calendar year and center; interrupted time-series description around March 2022 (descriptive, not causal).


8.2 Primary analysis (Aim 2)

Clone–censor–weight. Each eligible person is cloned into all three strategies at time zero. A clone is censored when its observed treatment deviates from its strategy (for example, a strategy C clone that fills methenamine on day 12). Censoring is modeled with pooled logistic regression on baseline and time-varying covariates (§5.8), giving stabilized inverse-probability-of-censoring weights10. Censoring at loss of eligible observation (L1–L3) is weighted in the same framework.
Estimands. Weighted mean cumulative counts and 12-month risks of UTI hospitalization by strategy. Contrasts: A vs. C (does methenamine reduce UTIs compared with no prophylaxis?) and A vs. B (how does it compare with antibiotic prophylaxis?). Report rate ratios and differences with bootstrap 95% CIs (resampling persons).
Per-protocol. Additionally censor at discontinuation or switching (§5.4) with time-varying weights.
Diagnostics. Weight distribution and truncation (1st/99th percentile as sensitivity), covariate balance after weighting, positivity by center and period.
Sample size. Determined by available data; contrasts are not described as formally powered. Report precision.



8.3 Vaginal estrogen trial (Aim 3)
Same machinery as Aim 2, restricted to women aged ≥50 (menopause proxy) meeting §4. Strategies: initiate vaginal estrogen within 30 days vs. not. Initiation of methenamine or antibiotic prophylaxis during follow-up is a time-varying covariate in the censoring weights for the per-protocol analysis; it is not a deviation in the intention-to-initiate analysis.

Open: #8 the age threshold.



8.4 Pre/post with a regression-to-the-mean reference (Aim 4)
Among methenamine initiators, compare treated UTI episode rates in the 12 months before and after initiation (Poisson or negative binomial with person-level clustering, as in the 2019 protocol). Repeat the identical calculation among eligible non-initiators anchored at the same qualifying-episode definition and matched on prior UTI count, time since transplant and calendar year. The difference between the two before/after ratios is the descriptive quantity of interest. Report this analysis as illustrating regression to the mean, not as a causal effect.


8.5 Effect modification and subgroups
Prespecified subgroups: sex, age ≥65, diabetes, time since transplant (<2 vs ≥2 years), urologic primary disease, ICD era.


8.6 Multiplicity

Open: #10 not yet specified.



8.7 Missing data

Open: #11 not yet specified.



8.8 Software
R, with USRDS files accessed through usRds. Record the usRds version or commit and the USRDS release for every result.

9. Sensitivity analyses

Negative-control outcome. An outcome that methenamine should not affect but that shares healthcare-contact pathways15. A non-null estimate flags residual confounding. Open: #9 the outcome; candidates are herpes zoster and hip fracture.
Quantitative bias analysis for exposure misclassification from out-of-plan fills (L4), using the low-income-subsidy restriction as an anchor.
Instrumental variable (exploratory). Center- or prescriber-level methenamine preference in the prior calendar year, as suggested in the 2019 protocol; report the instrument’s strength and assumptions explicitly.
Analyses named elsewhere in this plan: broader MPAB+MPO coverage (L1); restriction to low-income-subsidy enrollees (L4); varied prophylaxis and grace-period rules (L5, §5.4); era-specific estimates (L14); including recipients with chronic catheter or nephrostomy codes and sequential trials using every qualifying episode (§4); inpatient UTI in any diagnosis position (§7.1); weight truncation (§8.2).

10. Disclosure control
Governed by the USRDS data use agreement. Public code and code lists may be shared; restricted patient-level data may not. Suppress counts 1–10 and values derivable from complementary cells in all tables, figures and text; this may limit center- and subgroup-level reporting (L16).

11. Limitations to address in reporting
Restricted generalizability to recipients who keep Medicare FFS and Part D (L1–L3); residual confounding by indication (L11); exposure and outcome misclassification from dispensing-only data, out-of-plan fills and the absence of laboratory data (L4, L5, L9, L10).

Analytical scripts

R/main.R sources definitive scripts in dependency order.
Typical workflow: setup → cohort construction → processing → modeling → outputs.
Study-specific scripts may be grouped into subdirectories by analytical stage.
R/tables.R and R/figures.R may generate outputs directly or orchestrate specialized scripts.

Documentation

Document definitive analytical scripts with explanatory Quarto pages; exploratory scripts need not have pages.
Use Cryptococcus-cost-analysis as an example for Quarto supporting files, chunk imports, callouts, and formatting—not scientific methods.
Quarto source and rendered output locations may vary by project.

Outputs and version control

Track approved, nonrestricted outputs when useful for publication; otherwise retain them locally and exclude them from Git.
.gitignore: Exclude restricted data, credentials, caches, temporary files, and generated outputs unless intentionally tracked (e.g., .Rproj.user/, .Rhistory, .RData, .httr-oauth, .quarto/, cache/, figures/, tables/, *.quarto_ipynb); verify exclusions cover actual output paths without hiding necessary source or reference files.

title: Overview
text:
What this analysis does
This study will use the United States Renal Data System (USRDS), with linked Medicare Parts A, B and D claims, to describe how methenamine, prophylactic-dose antibiotics and vaginal estrogen are used after kidney transplantation. It will also compare starting methenamine, starting antibiotic prophylaxis, or starting neither among recipients with recurrent UTI.

title: Overview
text:
Methods
The comparisons are emulations of target trials, analyzed by cloning, censoring and weighting, with reporting following STROBE, RECORD and TARGET5–8. The analysis plan is the authoritative specification.

title: Overview
text:
Status
This is a planning repository. There is no active IRB approval, no data are in use, and the analysis plan is a draft that has not been adopted. Open decisions are marked in the plan and tracked in GitHub Issues.
Project documentsAGENTS.md Code

The project
This repository plans a study of methenamine hippurate, prophylactic-dose antibiotics and vaginal estrogen for recurrent urinary tract infection after kidney transplantation, using USRDS data with linked Medicare Parts A, B and D claims. It is a planning repository: there is no active IRB approval, no data are in use, and the analysis plan is a draft. The plan and, later, the code are published as a Quarto website.

analysis-plan.md is the source of truth for design. Code implements the plan; it does not redefine it. If code needs to depart from the plan, open a decision issue, or comment on the existing one, for the deciders. Once a decider has settled it (in the issue, or relayed there in their exact words), the plan change and the code can go in the same pull request, which closes the issue.
Deciders. Scientific decisions are made by: Vagish Hemmige, in every area. Anyone may open or contribute to a decision issue; only a decider settles it (see “Working with agents”).
This is an analysis project, not an R package. Do not add DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, roxygen, or pkgdown infrastructure, or apply CRAN conventions.
Default branch: master, protected. Changes reach it only through pull requests.

Data sources
Each source this project uses is listed below with the package that accesses it. Code that touches a source goes through its package. Do not write project-specific loading, cleaning, or definition code for something the package already does.











Source
Accessed through
Package documentation
Package maintained by
Access

USRDS standard analysis files, including linked Medicare claims, payer history and Part D drug events and enrollment (release as recorded for each result)

This team
Restricted (USRDS data use agreement)
None: code, documentation and synthetic data only



To allow more for a source, a person changes its row through a pull request, naming the agreement and section that permit it, the approved AI service, and exactly what agents may do. Agents never propose or make this change themselves, and nothing in personal instructions can grant it.
For every package:

Read its documentation before writing code for a source, including known issues. Behavior that sets the cohort, an exposure, an outcome, or a denominator is checked in the documentation, not assumed from a function’s name.

For packages this team maintains:

Facts about the source belong in the package’s documentation, not in this file. If the package lacks something this project needs to know, add it there or open an issue there.
Problems belong in the package. If a function is wrong or does not quite do what the plan needs, open an issue in its repository. Fix it in the package (preferred when generally useful) or wrap it here with a code comment linking the issue, and remove the wrapper once the issue is fixed.

For external packages:

Work around problems here. Wrap the function in R/functions.R with a comment explaining the problem and linking any upstream issue. Reporting a bug upstream is an external communication; the person directing the work decides whether to file it.
Facts about the source that this project relies on (definitions, release quirks, suppression rules) go in references/ with a citation to the provider’s documentation, or in the plan when they shape a decision.

For a source with no package: one loading script records the download URL, the release or access date, and any processing. Verify its variables against the provider’s documentation for that release.

Exploration and definitive analysis
Exploration is welcome on branches or forks. Experimental scripts need not be sourced from R/main.R or have Quarto pages, and their findings are labelled preliminary. A script becomes part of the definitive analysis when it is sourced from R/main.R; from then on every rule below applies to it.

R scripts

Running the analysis. Run R/main.R from the project root. It sources the other scripts in dependency order; ARCHITECTURE.md describes what each does.
One job per script. When you add a definitive script, source it from main.R at the right point and update ARCHITECTURE.md in the same pull request.
Header comment. Each script begins with what it does, which objects it needs from earlier scripts, and what it produces.
Constants, libraries, and code lists live in R/setup.R. Other scripts do not call library(), re-source setup.R, or hard-code values. Any number a reader might want to change (a window, a year, a threshold, a ratio) is a named constant there.
Helper functions go in R/functions.R. A function takes its inputs as arguments and does not read global objects.
No side effects outside the project. No setwd(), absolute paths, or writes outside the project. Restricted data are located only through their access package’s configuration.
No results in the repository. No script (exploratory or definitive) or comment, commit message, issue, pull-request text or review report contains results, counts or data values from restricted data unless they are cleared for release. Check before every commit and post, since a public repository publishes everything pushed to it, on any branch.

Chunk labels
Scripts are divided into labelled sections so Quarto pages can show the code without copying it:
## ---- <step-name>

Every logical step has a label. A label covers the code from its line to the next label.
Labels are kebab-case, describe the step, and are unique across all scripts; a duplicate silently picks up the wrong code.
Search the .qmd files before renaming or deleting a label.
Labels are comments and never change what the code does.

Variable labels
Label analysis variables with human-readable descriptions (for example labelled::set_variable_labels(), or the access package’s labelling functions where it has them). Label each derived variable where it is created, with units, price year, and windows where they apply.

Quarto website
The site documents the code. It does not run the analysis.

_quarto.yml, index.qmd, 404.qmd (the page GitHub Pages shows for a missing address) and styles.css sit at the root; quarto/ has one page per definitive script, named after it, plus the Background, Study design and methods, About and project-document pages. The custom-callout extension in _extensions/ provides the Rcode, Results and Pending callouts.
Visual cues. Each kind of page has one sidebar icon, coloured by styles.css, and pages mark the same kind of content with the callout of that colour: background book (blue); study design and methods diagram-3 (orange); R code laptop (pink, Rcode 💻); results clipboard-data (green, Results 📊); project documents file-earmark-ruled (grey). Give every new page the icon of its kind.
Provisional content. quarto/_pending.lua highlights in yellow every paragraph that starts with Decision pending: or, in the plan, Open:, and any [text]{.pending}, and adds a ⏳ Pending callout to pages that have a mark. Mark only what an open decision could change, and remove the mark when the decision is settled.
Project documents. analysis-plan.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, AGENTS.md and REPOSITORY-BLUEPRINT.md are shown on the site by pages in quarto/ that only include the root file, which stays the one source: edit the root file, not the page.
Each page loads its script with knitr::read_chunk("../R/<script>.R") in a hidden chunk and shows each labelled section with #| eval: false, with prose explaining what the section does and why. Pages link to the script on GitHub and to the scripts it depends on.
Never evaluate analysis code in the site. Pages render without restricted data. Only the read_chunk() imports, the Architecture page’s chunk that reads ARCHITECTURE.md, site helpers that read code or text, and results pages that read cleared outputs run.
The site renders to docs/, which is not committed: a GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/publish.yml) renders it on every push to master and publishes it to the gh-pages branch, which GitHub Pages serves. On a pull request the workflow only renders, as a check that every page builds. When you add a script, add its page and sidebar entry in the same pull request.
Reader comments. The issue-comments extension lets readers highlight text and comment, after entering the shared passcode; the relay files each comment as an issue in this repository.
Prose must match the code. If a change alters what a section does, update its explanation in the same pull request.

Outputs

Tables and figures are exported by R/tables.R and R/figures.R to tables/ and figures/. Gitignored until USRDS review before publication clears them for release, under the disclosure rules below, because they come from restricted data: agents may not open them (see Restricted data).
Published figures need alt text.
README.Rmd is the source of README.md; edit the .Rmd and re-knit.

Restricted data (applies to everyone)
The Access column of “Data sources” says which sources are restricted. For each restricted source:

Never commit data, extracts, or saved objects or outputs derived from patient-level records. Keep data outside the repository, and check .gitignore before adding a new output type.
AI agents never read restricted data. Anything an agent opens, prints, or summarizes is sent to the model provider. Agents do not open data files or patient-level objects, print rows, or display identifiers, person-level dates, or small geographies. Agents also do not open outputs from restricted data that are not yet cleared for release (for example tables/ and figures/ while they are ignored). Agents write code, review it, and run it on synthetic data; results on real data are produced by an authorized person. The only exception is what the Data sources table explicitly allows for a source, and only within those words.
Synthetic data are built in code, labelled as synthetic, and never derived from real records.
Disclosure. Follow the USRDS data use agreement: no counts 1–10 in tables, figures, flowchart boxes, risk tables or prose, including counts recoverable from complementary cells or by subtraction. Counts that have appeared in grant applications are not repeated here unless there is a reason to publish them. Check every output before it leaves the approved environment, including scripts, comments, commit messages, issues, pull-request text and review reports (see R scripts).
Credentials and paid APIs. Never commit keys, tokens, or .Renviron. Ask before paid, bulk, or uncached API calls. Before a paid batch, make one call with the exact package version, model and settings, and check the result before running the rest. Which model or service version to use is the person’s choice; an agent proposes, with the cost if known, and does not switch it on its own.

Coding conventions

Cohort flow uses the flowchart package, so the STROBE flow diagram and the analytic cohort come from the same code. Every inclusion or exclusion goes through fc_filter(), in the plan’s order. Never remove people from the cohort outside the flowchart. Record-level processing (cleaning claims, choosing among a person’s records) is fine. An analysis that uses fewer people than the cohort (complete cases, a subgroup) reports its own number with that analysis. The cohort used downstream is the data from the final step (fc_view(what = "data")). Flowchart labels are built from constants in setup.R.
Code lists carry each code’s category, code system and version, and matching rule (exact or prefix). Check every code against the official code set. Never invent codes, variables, files, or definitions.
Joins use join_by() with an explicit relationship where possible. After every interval join and every join of records to people, assert that rows did not multiply, and decide deliberately what happens to unmatched rows.
Dates and windows are written as inclusive offsets from the index date, matching the plan, and the edges are tested on synthetic data.
Code that turns model output into reported numbers lives in named functions in R/functions.R, tested on synthetic data with a known answer.
Package APIs: read the help page and NEWS for the installed version before calling a package; don’t write calls from memory. A test that fakes a package checks only our own logic, so call the real package once (synthetic data, or one cheap call) before relying on the code.
Style: readable for a clinician-analyst who learned R from online guides: pipes and dplyr/tidyr verbs, case_when(), loops over names or named lists rather than the apply family, Reduce or positional indexing. Required base R goes in a named, tested function. Tidyverse layout; style changes in their own commits.

Checks for any change
Check the items that apply before opening a pull request.

Plan: does the change implement the plan as written, and does it leave every open decision open?
Data sources: does it use the access package’s functions, and does their documented behavior match what the plan needs?
Package APIs: for new or changed calls to a package, does the pull request name the installed version and the help page or NEWS entry relied on?
Cohort: do the flowchart steps’ order, denominators, and labels match their conditions, and can each count be reproduced from code?
Joins and denominators: no unintended row multiplication; missing, suppressed, and zero kept distinct.
Reported numbers: does each estimate match the plan’s estimand, and do tables, figures, and site prose say what the code actually computes?
Structure: is ARCHITECTURE.md current; are chunk labels unique and found by their pages; does every definitive script have a page and sidebar entry; does any site chunk run analysis code? Only the hidden read_chunk() imports, the Architecture page’s chunk that reads ARCHITECTURE.md, site helpers that read code or text, and results pages reading outputs cleared for release, run.
Disclosure: search every changed tracked file, and the commit messages and pull-request text, for dates, record IDs, names, absolute paths and numbers that could come from restricted data. Read each hit in context; legitimate ones (plan dates, deciders’ names, synthetic examples) stay.
Execution: does main.R run in a fresh session with relative paths; are any saved intermediates or caches stale?

Project-specific checks

Eligible observation: does each day counted as observed have MPAB and Part D enrollment together, as the plan defines it, and is loss of either handled as the plan says?
Drug exposure: are prophylaxis and treatment fills told apart by the plan’s dose and supply rules, are single-agent methenamine products separated from combination products, and are same-day fills collapsed?
Time zero and arms: is time zero the end of the qualifying UTI episode, and is each clone’s strategy judged only from information available by that day?
ICD transition: are ICD-9-CM and ICD-10-CM code lists applied by the plan’s date rule?

Working with agents

Autonomy. The person directing an agent sets its working style (review only, step by step, or hands-off) in their own instructions, and may add stricter rules; those take precedence. Without a style, an agent works step by step. At most, an agent may edit code and documentation, add scripts and tests, run code and render the site on synthetic data, and commit to a branch and open a pull request.
Decisions. Anyone, including an agent, may add options and evidence to a decision issue. A decider states the choice in the issue. Agents implement decisions; they never choose among options on their own, in the issue, the plan, or the code.
Every agent, under any autonomy: never merges a pull request; follows the restricted-data rules; asks before running the full pipeline or making expensive calls; shows a person the exact text before posting or sending anything as them, unless that person’s own instructions waive this; and proposes another way of writing something already agreed before committing it.
Pull requests opened by an agent are focused. Each says which plan section or issue it addresses, what was checked, and whether by running code on synthetic data or by reading only. Synthetic results are never described as results.
References: cite the source documentation and literature used, in references.bib.

title: About
text:
This study asks whether methenamine hippurate, compared with antibiotic prophylaxis or with neither, reduces recurrent urinary tract infection after kidney transplantation. It is at the planning stage: there is no active IRB approval, no data are in use, and the analysis plan is a draft.

title: About
text:
This repository
R/main.R will run the scripts in order. For now the scripts are the R Analysis Workflow plugin’s starter files, which run on a few synthetic numbers and touch no data. The study will use the United States Renal Data System (USRDS), including its linked Medicare claims, loaded through the usRds package. USRDS data are restricted under a data use agreement, so they will never be in the repository; the code will run only where an authorized person has access to them.
Contributions follow the rules in AGENTS.md; known issues and open decisions are tracked in Issues.

title: About
text:
How this website was created
The site is built with Quarto from the analysis scripts themselves. Each code page imports the labelled sections of its script from R/ and shows them with an explanation; the site never runs the analysis, so it is built without the analysis data. A GitHub Actions workflow renders and publishes it whenever master changes.
The repository follows the R Analysis Workflow plugin and the layout of Cryptococcus-missed-diagnosis-USRDS. AI assistants may help draft and review code and documentation. They never see USRDS data, they work on synthetic data only, and changes reach master through pull requests a person reviews and merges.
Four documents describe the project. In short: the plan is the scientific intent, the architecture is the workflow as implemented, and AGENTS.md holds the rules for working together.

Analysis plan: what the analysis is meant to do, and why. The question, the population, the methods, and the open decisions. Code implements it and does not redefine it.
Architecture: how the code does it. The scripts, the order they run in, what each needs and produces, and how data flow between them.
AGENTS.md: how people and AI assistants work on the project. Rules for restricted data, coding, checks, proposing changes and getting a person’s approval.
Repository blueprint: the layout every project of this kind starts from, which the architecture document then describes as built.

title: Clinical background
text:
Single-center studies in kidney transplant recipients report fewer urinary tract infections (UTIs) after methenamine hippurate is started1–3. Each compared patients before and after starting, without a comparison group. Prophylaxis tends to be started when infections are at their most frequent, so a later decline is expected from regression to the mean alone, whatever the drug does.
In women with recurrent UTI who had not had a transplant, the ALTAR randomized trial found methenamine hippurate noninferior to daily antibiotic prophylaxis4, and a companion analysis examined its cost-effectiveness5. No randomized trial has been done in kidney transplant recipients.






References

1. Hollyer I, Varias F, Ho B, Ison MG. Safety and efficacy of methenamine hippurate for the prevention of recurrent urinary tract infections in adult renal transplant recipients: A single center, retrospective study. Transplant Infectious Disease. 2019;21(3):e13063. doi:10.1111/tid.13063


2. Sweiss H, Bhayana S, Hall R, Nelson J, Kincaide E. Methenamine for recurrent urinary tract infections in solid organ transplantation. Progress in Transplantation. 2022;32(1):67-72. doi:10.1177/15269248211064880


3. Quintero Cardona O, Hemmige VS, Puius YA. Methenamine hippurate may have particular benefit in preventing recurrent urinary tract infections in diabetic renal transplant recipients. Transplant Infectious Disease. 2020;22(2):e13247. doi:10.1111/tid.13247


4. Harding C, Mossop H, Homer T, et al. Alternative to prophylactic antibiotics for the treatment of recurrent urinary tract infections in women: Multicentre, open label, randomised, non-inferiority trial. BMJ. 2022;376:e068229. doi:10.1136/bmj-2021-068229


5. King W, Homer T, Harding C, et al. Cost-effectiveness of methenamine hippurate compared with antibiotic prophylaxis for the management of recurrent urinary tract infections in secondary care: A multicentre, open-label, randomised, non-inferiority trial. BMJ Open. 2024;14(4):e074445. doi:10.1136/bmjopen-2023-074445
